# FDG9056

> DO NOT set default values of dependency properties explicitly in code; instead, set them in metadata.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 9.3.1 Dependency Property Design.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG9056
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: draft

Message: Set the default value of the dependency property '{0}' in its metadata, not in the constructor

FDG9056 reports, in an instance constructor of a class derived from DependencyObject, an assignment to the CLR property of one of the class's own dependency properties (found as for FDG9054), or a SetValue call with its field, when the value is one that metadata can hold: a constant, default, typeof, or a static field or property (String.Empty in the body). A value computed for each instance, such as a constructor argument or a new object, is not a default that metadata could hold and is not reported, so coverage is partial; so are assignments in lambdas and in other methods. The constructor of the FDG9058 example, which sets a constant through SetValue, is reported. The fix moves the value into the PropertyMetadata of the registration; there is no code fix.

## From the book

If you set a property default explicitly, you might prevent that property from being set by some implicit means, such as a styling.

```csharp
public class TextButton : DependencyObject {

  public TextButton(){
    // do not set DP default values explicitly
    Text = String.Empty;  // this is bad!
  }

  public static readonly DependencyProperty TextProperty =
    DependencyProperty.Register(
        "Text",
        typeof(string),
        typeof(TextButton),
        new PropertyMetadata(String.Empty)); // this is good!
}
```
